title: 🎓 Section 3 — Academic Discussions

sections.heading: What to expect
sections.body:
Section 3 has 2–3 speakers in an educational context:
• Two students discussing an assignment
• A tutor giving feedback to a student
• A group of students planning a project
• A student and supervisor discussing research

This section is noticeably harder than Sections 1–2. The speakers express opinions, speculate, and agree/disagree with each other.

sections.heading: What makes it hard
sections.body:
• Speakers CHANGE THEIR MINDS — "Actually, I think you're right..." → follow who changes opinion
• Speakers CONTRADICT each other — the question tests who holds which view
• Questions test ATTITUDE and OPINION — not just facts
• Answer options often paraphrase what was said very differently

highlight: Section 3 multiple choice often has options that are "almost right." The difference is usually one key word — "always" vs "sometimes", "main" vs "only".

question: In Section 3, you hear: Student A: "I think we should focus mainly on the economic impact." Student B: "I agree — and actually, the social impact is just as important." What is Student B's view?
options: Both economic and social impacts are important
correct: Both economic and social impacts are important
explanation:
Student B AGREES with A about economic impact ("I agree") and then ADDS social impact ("just as important").

This type of opinion-tracking is the core skill for Section 3. You must follow:
• Who says what
• Whether they agree, disagree, or add nuance
• Whether they change their mind

question: Which strategy is most important for Section 3 multiple choice?
options: Write every word the speakers say
Focus only on what the first speaker says
Listen for agreements, disagreements, and opinion changes
Skip difficult questions and guess later
correct: Listen for agreements, disagreements, and opinion changes
explanation:
Section 3 tests social/academic interaction — not just factual recall.

Key phrases to track:
• Agreement: "Exactly", "I think you're right", "That's a good point"
• Disagreement: "Actually, I'm not sure about that", "I'd push back on that"
• Opinion change: "Having thought about it...", "You've changed my mind"
